Rebuilding a first-year engineering course on GitHub · Purdue FYE (ENGR 131)

children.label: Rebuilding a first-year engineering course on GitHub · Purdue FYE (ENGR 131)

children.value: ENGR 131 used to reach students as separate materials in each of its 20+ sections, so every fix had to be made more than once. I proposed moving the course onto one version-controlled platform built on GitHub, Codespaces, and Jupyter Book, and I led the technical build: a site that GitHub Actions compiles and deploys, with Gradescope autograders that pull their tests from the same repository. The rewritten course
shipped for Fall 2026 and is live now
. It covers professional development, Excel, AI, Python, and a semester-long team design project, and
30 of its assignments are graded automatically
. I shared content authorship with the curriculum team, and wrote a prose-style checker (62 tests) that keeps writing from several authors consistent.
Jupyter Book v2 · MyST Markdown · GitHub Actions · GitHub Codespaces · Gradescope · Python
Hardening a production autograder · Purdue FYE (ENGR 131)

children.label: Hardening a production autograder · Purdue FYE (ENGR 131)

children.value: that grades ~2,600 first-year engineering students each semester, a shared course system I help maintain. My work: rebuilt the SSH deploy-key pipeline to fail loudly instead of silently shipping broken grading; added Excel-submission autograding; rewrote the late-penalty engine to read deadlines straight from Gradescope’s own submission metadata (flat, timezone-correct, fail-open); and authored the technical and authoring documentation the TA team uses. It runs on a clone-at-grade-time model, so a test fix deploys on merge with no re-upload.

A private photo cloud for my family

children.label: A private photo cloud for my family

children.value: Self-hosted photo infrastructure that gets my family off big-tech storage without making sharing worse. Photos live on my own ZFS-backed

server and reach relatives through a zero-trust tunnel, each on a scoped subdomain of their own. There are no accounts to create and nothing to install. The delivery surface is the part most self-hosted setups skip. I converted cheap Amazon Fire tablets into single-purpose photo frames, stripping the stock OS down to a debloated kiosk build locked to one app and routed home over a VPN, then prototyped the wood enclosures myself and commissioned the finished frames. They run unattended in houses I can’t reach, for people who will never open a settings menu.
